research_sources: Wikipedia: Silver hallmarks, Sterling silver, Silver plating, EPNS, Old Sheffield Plate, Reed & Barton
ASCAS (Association of Small Collectors of Antique Silver) references

925.name: Sterling Silver
925.description: Most common sterling mark. 925 parts per thousand pure silver, 75 parts copper alloy
925.appearance: Numbers '925' stamped or engraved. Can be shallow on plated items, deeper on solid
925.history: First legal definition appeared in 1275 during Edward I's reign. Approximately millesimal fineness of 926
925.value: Standard for quality silver items. Post-1868 American standard

STERLING.name: Sterling
STERLING.description: American sterling mark. Often found on flatware, holloware
STERLING.appearance: Word 'STERLING' stamped in capital letters. Sometimes '925/1000'
STERLING.history: Adopted as US standard in 1868. Before this, 'coin silver' (90.3%) was common
STERLING.value: Indicates solid sterling silver in American items

800.name: Continental Silver
800.description: European standard. Common in German and French silver
800.appearance: Numbers '800' stamped. May have additional marks like cross pattee
800.value: Lower purity but still solid silver. Common in continental European items

835.name: French Silver
835.description: French standard for silver. Accompanied by Minerva head mark
835.appearance: Numbers '835' stamped, often with eagle head or Minerva profile symbol
835.history: French 2nd Standard. French also has 1st Standard at 950/1000
835.value: Solid French silver. Minerva head indicates post-1838

958.name: Britannia Silver
958.description: Higher purity British standard. Rare, valuable
958.appearance: Numbers '958' stamped. Often accompanied by Britannia figure
958.history: Obligatory in Britain 1697-1720 to prevent coin melting. Optional standard thereafter
958.value: Higher purity than sterling. Collectible, especially antique pieces

999.name: Fine Silver
999.description: Pure silver. Rare in antique items, more common in modern bullion
999.value: Highest purity. Not common in antique flatware or holloware

COIN SILVER.name: Coin Silver
COIN SILVER.description: Pre-1837 American standard. Made from melted coins
COIN SILVER.appearance: Words 'COIN SILVER' or 'PURE COIN' stamped. Sometimes just '903'
COIN SILVER.history: Pre-1868 US standard. Purity varied from 750 to 900 millesimal fineness
COIN SILVER.value: Historically significant. Pre-1837 pieces can be valuable

EPNS.name: Electroplated Nickel Silver
EPNS.description: NOT solid silver. Thin layer of silver over nickel alloy base (60% copper, 20% nickel, 20% zinc)
EPNS.appearance: Letters 'EPNS' or 'E.P.N.S.' stamped. Can be in decorative shield
EPNS.history: Electroplating process patented 1840 by George and Henry Elkington in Birmingham
EPNS.value: Has collectible value but NOT solid silver. Pre-1900 pieces more valuable
EPNS.identification: Nickel silver base is non-magnetic. Shows brass/copper color at wear points

EP.name: Electroplated
EP.description: Electroplated base metal. Not solid silver
EP.value: Lower value than EPNS. Common in later items

SILVER PLATED.name: Silver Plated
SILVER PLATED.description: Thin layer of silver over base metal. Has value but not solid silver
SILVER PLATED.appearance: Words 'SILVER PLATED' or 'SP' stamped. UK law prohibits calling it just 'silver'
SILVER PLATED.value: Collectible but lower value than solid silver

A1.name: American Silver Plated
A1.description: American plated standard. Not solid silver

SHEFFIELD PLATE.name: Old Sheffield Plate (OSP)
SHEFFIELD PLATE.description: Fused silver and copper sheets (1740s-1840s). NOT electroplated
SHEFFIELD PLATE.appearance: No 'EP' marks. Shows copper bleeding at wear points. Bluish cast vs electroplate
SHEFFIELD PLATE.history: Invented by Thomas Boulsover 1740s. Replaced by electroplating ~1840
SHEFFIELD PLATE.value: Can be very valuable (pre-1800 pieces). Collectors seek genuine OSP
SHEFFIELD PLATE.identification: Look for copper bleeding at wear points. Soldered joints indicate OSP. Distinctive bluish lustre

lion_passant.name: British Sterling Mark
lion_passant.description: Walking lion symbol. Indicates 925 sterling silver in British hallmarks
lion_passant.appearance: Lion shown walking, head facing left. One of most recognizable hallmarks
lion_passant.history: Used since 1300s. Standard for British sterling silver

lion_head_crowned.name: Britannia Standard Mark
lion_head_crowned.description: Crowned lion head. Indicates Britannia standard (958) silver

Birmingham.description: Second largest. Anchor symbol (same as London but different shield shape)

Glasgow.description: Scottish assay office. Tree with three fish

date_letters.description: British hallmarks include a letter indicating year of assay. Each office has its own alphabet cycle with different font styles per decade
date_letters.how_to_read: Find the date letter (usually small, separate from other marks). Match font style and shield shape to assay office calendar
date_letters.note: Date letters change style each decade. Same letter in different shield shapes = different years

maker_marks.description: Two-letter initials or symbols identifying the silversmith. Usually inside an escutcheon (shield shape)

duty_marks.description: Profile of reigning monarch. Shows tax paid to Crown
duty_marks.note: Not found on items after 1890. George III, William IV, Victoria profiles

tally_marks.description: Unique mark of journeyman finishing apprenticeship. Record for payment
tally_marks.note: Rare. Found on very old pieces

french_minerva.name: French Silver Standard
french_minerva.description: Minerva (goddess) head in profile. French assay mark for silver
french_minerva.appearance: Head of Minerva facing right. Sometimes with numeral 1 (950) or 2 (800)
french_minerva.history: Used since 1838. Replaced earlier eagle head marks

french_eagle_head.name: French Export Mark
french_eagle_head.description: Mercury head for export silver. Indicates millesimal fineness number

german_cross_pattee.name: German Silver Cross
german_cross_pattee.description: Cross with decorated arms. German hallmark for silver

swiss_maiden_head.name: Swiss Silver Mark
swiss_maiden_head.description: Maiden's head symbol. Swiss assay office mark

hungarian_diana.name: Austria-Hungary Silver Mark
hungarian_diana.description: Crowned head of Diana within frame. Frame shape indicates fineness
hungarian_diana.appearance: Diana head in geometric frame. Concave lines = 140, straight = 150, convex = 160
hungarian_diana.example: Petal frame (5×160) = 800 fineness. Hexagonal frame = 900 fine

Reed & Barton.mark: RB or Reed & Barton with pattern number
Reed & Barton.value: Quality American silver. Sterling pieces valuable. Bankrupt 2015
Reed & Barton.notes: Produced Olympic medals 1996. Merged with Dominick & Haff 1928
Reed & Barton.patterns: Many sterling and silverplate patterns. Pattern numbers help identify value

Tiffany & Co..mark: TIFFANY & CO. with pattern number or year code
Tiffany & Co..value: Extremely valuable. Museum quality pieces command high prices
Tiffany & Co..notes: Most famous American silversmith. Sterling and silverplate

International Silver Co..value: Common but collectible. Quality silver plate and sterling
International Silver Co..notes: Merged several companies. Major American producer

Wm. Rogers & Co..mark: WR & Co or Rogers with various patterns
Wm. Rogers & Co..value: Common silver plate. Some sterling pieces valuable
Wm. Rogers & Co..notes: Many patterns produced. Check for 925 mark to confirm sterling

Silvertown Silver Co..value: American silver plate. Pattern numbers help identify

Gorham.mark: GORHAM with pattern number or Greek key mark
Gorham.value: High-quality American silver. Sterling pieces very valuable
Gorham.notes: Known for Art Nouveau and Arts & Crafts designs

wear_points.description: Check edges, tips of forks, backs of spoons. Plated items show brass/copper base metal at high-wear points
wear_points.what_to_look_for: Yellow/golden color showing through silver at edges or tips = plated

weight_test.description: Solid silver is significantly heavier than plated items of same size

magnet_test.description: Silver is non-magnetic. If magnet sticks, it's steel core = plated or fake
magnet_test.note: Some base metals (brass, copper, nickel silver) also non-magnetic, so no stick doesn't prove solid

ice_test.description: Silver conducts heat fastest. Ice cube melts faster on solid silver than plated
ice_test.note: Requires comparison for accuracy. Best done with known items

tone_test.description: Tap two silver items together. Solid silver produces clear, long ringing tone. Plated items produce duller sound
tone_test.note: Requires experience. Best learned by comparing known solid vs plated items

shallow_stamping.description: Fake hallmarks often stamped too shallow or with wrong font
shallow_stamping.how_to_check: Run finger over mark. Real hallmarks are crisp, deep, precise

wrong_placement.description: Fake marks often in wrong location or too prominent
wrong_placement.real_pattern: Real hallmarks are subtle, usually on underside/bottom

modern_fonts.description: Antique items should have period-appropriate stamping. Modern fonts on 'antique' = reproduction
modern_fonts.note: Font styles changed over centuries. Research period-appropriate marks

too_perfect.description: Real hallmarks show slight variations. Perfectly identical marks on multiple items may indicate modern reproduction
too_perfect.note: Hand-stamped marks have slight variations. Machine-made marks are too uniform

wrong_combinations.description: Hallmark combinations that don't match historical periods
wrong_combinations.example: Lion passant with 925 mark = wrong (lion passant is British, 925 is American/European)

silver_wash.description: Very thin silver coating over base metal. Wears off quickly
silver_wash.identification: Shows base metal at any wear point, very light weight

sterling_over_base.description: Solid silver top over base metal bottom (common in bowls)
sterling_over_base.identification: Check inside bowl - if different mark or no mark, may be silver top only

reproductions.description: Modern items made to look antique
reproductions.identification: Perfect condition, no wear, modern maker marks, shiny without patina
reproductions.note: Many patterns reproduced. Check weight, mark quality, and wear patterns

base_metal_with_fake_marks.description: Brass or nickel silver stamped with fake 925 marks
base_metal_with_fake_marks.identification: Magnet test, weight test, wear points showing base metal

weighted_silver.description: Silver shell filled with lead or other heavy metal to simulate solid silver weight
weighted_silver.identification: X-ray required for definitive test. Sound test may reveal hollow nature

look_for: EPNS, Silver Plated, EP = plated (not solid)
No marks = could be anything, test further

step_2.method: Compare to similar known items. Solid silver feels heavy for size

step_3.method: Silver doesn't attract magnets. If magnet sticks = base metal core

step_4.method: Check edges, tips. Plated items show base metal color at wear points

step_5.method: Look for silversmith initials or company names. Famous makers add value

forks.marks_location: underside of handle or back of tines
identification_tips: Check underside of handle for marks
Look for wear points showing base metal
Solid silver spoons have deeper feel

knives.marks_location: underside of handle or blade tang
identification_tips: Silver handles on steel blades common in silverplate
Large pieces more likely to be valuable if sterling

pattern_identification.description: Each pattern has unique design. Pattern numbers help identify value and replacement pieces
pattern_identification.how_to_identify: Compare with pattern guides online. Note: pattern alone doesn't indicate silver content - check for 925 mark

identification_tips: Check inside for different marks (may be silver top only)
Look for copper bleeding if OSP
Large trays more valuable if sterling

pre_1965.description: US dimes, quarters, half dollars minted before 1965 are 90% silver

silver_dollars.description: Various US silver dollars. Morgan dollars (1878-1921) most collectible

identification_tips: Check date - pre-1965 US coins are silver
Look for mint marks (small letters near date)
Weight and size should match specifications
Edge should be reeded (grooved), not smooth

natural_patina.description: Silver naturally tarnishes to dark gray/black. This is normal and can be polished
natural_patina.note: Heavy patina doesn't mean low value - many collectors prefer original patina

polishing_damage.description: Over-polished silver loses detail and value. Check for smooth, featureless surfaces
polishing_damage.note: Some wear is normal and expected on antique items

dents_and_damage.description: Minor dents may be acceptable on functional items. Cracks, holes significantly reduce value
dents_and_damage.note: Holloware with dents may still have good silver content

missing_parts.description: Missing lids, handles, or pieces reduce value significantly
missing_parts.note: Matching sets are worth much more than individual pieces
